title: Review Document Production Set for Attorney-Client Privilege Designations — Privilege Log and Recommendation Memo

blind.coverage: Read all 48 criteria and the instructions. Read these documents in full: privilege-review-protocol, nandakumar-legal-risk-email, emmerich-forward-to-moritani, emmerich-reformulation-email, slack-product-reformulation, rennick-tsao-labeling-email, rennick-handwritten-note, board-audit-committee-deck, bridger-to-cascade-counsel, frey-personal-email-notes, litigation-strategy-memo, pemberton-invoice, pemberton-opinion-letter, inadvertent-production-clawback, and draft-privilege-log (all sheets). Skimmed or searched these with grep: competitive-market-analysis (header, authorship, distribution, stamps), first-rfp-set (privilege-log instructions and requests about labeling opinions), litigation-hold-notice (header and distribution). I ran an automated 7-word overlap comparison between the strategy memo and the board deck to test the "near-verbatim" premise. I did not open the harness system prompt or judge prompt beyond what the task text describes. The legal authorities below come from general knowledge. None was retrieved or read in this session, so each is marked verified=false. The CourtListener tools were not used.

findings.title: Board deck slides 7-8 do not reproduce the Frey memo near-verbatim; they paraphrase it and in places contradict it
findings.explanation: C-006 passes only if the report identifies a "near-verbatim reproduction of paragraphs" from DOC_005 in slides 7-8. C-007 assumes the same verbatim incorporation. The record does not support this. An n-gram comparison found no shared 7-word run outside the case caption and boilerplate phrases like "100% Natural front-of-pack labeling is misleading." The slides summarize the memo in bullets, and they diverge from it on substance. The deck calls class-certification risk "moderate-to-significant" where the memo says "high" (65-75%). The deck says counsel recommends "exploring early mediation," but the memo advises starting settlement talks only after class-certification briefing is underway. A careful reviewer who compared the documents would say the deck incorporates or summarizes work product, not that it copies it verbatim. That reviewer is exposed to a FAIL on C-006. A report that calls the slides verbatim would be rewarded for an inaccurate factual claim. Only the protocol's hypothetical ("if work product content is incorporated verbatim") and a draft-log note that the deck "may have incorporated some of this analysis" point toward verbatim copying.

evidence.quote: slides 7-8, contains near-verbatim reproduction of paragraphs from DOC_005
Preliminary assessment: Plaintiff's claims present moderate-to-significant risk at the class certification stage
Assessment:** Class certification risk is **high**.
recommends aggressive defense of class certification motion while exploring early mediation to manage exposure
We recommend initiating confidential settlement discussions only after class certification briefing is underway
NB mentioned Board presentation may have incorporated some of this analysis.

findings.suggested_fix: Replace "near-verbatim reproduction of paragraphs" with "incorporates or summarizes the analysis and conclusions of DOC_005 (litigation risk assessment and defense strategy)." In C-007, change "verbatim" to "incorporating attorney work product."

findings.title: C-014 requires saying DOC_003 was cc'd to Fontaine and Chu, but the email header shows only Tomas Brandt as cc
findings.explanation: The DOC_003 header lists Rennick as the only To recipient and Tomas Brandt, Director of QA, as the only Cc. Leah Fontaine and Derek Chu are not in the header. The body mentions them by name and gives them tasks. The claim that they were cc'd comes from the draft privilege log's notes, a secondary work paper, and the log contradicts the email itself. C-014 requires the report to find that DOC_003 "was cc'd to ... specifically Leah Fontaine and Derek Chu." A reviewer who relies on the primary document would say the cc was to Brandt, a non-lawyer, and might note that the body addresses the two analysts. That report risks a FAIL. A report that copies the draft log's error passes. A careful reviewer would also flag the conflict between the log and the email, and the criterion does not account for that.

findings.title: The email forwarded in DOC_009 is a different message from DOC_008, which undercuts C-005's premise that DOC_008's full content was disclosed
findings.explanation: C-005 assumes DOC_008 is at risk "since the full content was disclosed to Dr. Moritani." C-003 likewise refers to "the forwarding of DOC_008's legal analysis." The two documents are different messages. DOC_008 was sent at 14:47 PDT under a longer subject line, opens "Following up on your question from our call last Tuesday," and cites a "1991 advisory opinion." The original quoted in DOC_009 was sent at 4:42 PM PDT, has the subject "Legal Risk Assessment of Natural Claim," opens "Thank you for reaching out," and cites "1993 guidance." The two cover similar substance, but their text is entirely different. A careful reviewer could reasonably conclude that DOC_009 waived privilege in the forwarded 4:42 PM email and that DOC_008 is a separate communication. Extrajudicial disclosure generally waives privilege only in what was disclosed, not the whole subject matter. That reviewer could therefore treat DOC_008 as privileged and fail C-005. Many reviewers would still flag overlap risk, so this is arguable rather than certain.

authorities.citation: Fed. R. Evid. 502(a) & Advisory Committee Note (2008)
authorities.proposition: Subject-matter waiver is limited to intentional disclosures in a federal proceeding where fairness requires it; extrajudicial disclosure ordinarily waives only what was disclosed

findings.suggested_fix: Make DOC_009's embedded text match DOC_008. findings.title: C-019 fails any DOC_006 log entry that says the advice concerned labeling compliance, which blurs subject matter with substance
findings.explanation: C-019 fails a DOC_006 log entry that reveals "the advice concerned whether the 'Natural' labeling was compliant" or that the advice was about whether the labeling "complied." The protocol's own approved examples, which C-038 endorses, include "legal analysis regarding product labeling compliance" and "legal opinion on regulatory compliance matters." Rule 26(b)(5)(A) and RFP Instruction 4(e) require the subject matter to be described "in sufficient detail to allow assessment of the privilege claim." Plaintiff's RFP No. 87 asks for exactly such labeling-compliance opinions from outside counsel, and slide 8 of the deck already discloses that Pemberton gave a June 2021 compliance opinion. An entry such as "legal opinion regarding compliance of product labeling claims" states the subject matter without revealing Pemberton's conclusion. Different judges could split on whether that counts as "whether labeling complied." The distinction between protected substance and required subject matter is not operationalized.

"Email from in-house counsel to outside litigation counsel providing legal analysis regarding product labeling compliance."
(e) the subject matter described in sufficient detail to allow assessment of the privilege claim without revealing privileged content

findings.suggested_fix: Fail only entries that disclose the conclusion or risk assessment (for example, that the claim was non-compliant or risky, or the threshold analysis). Say explicitly that stating the subject, such as a labeling or regulatory compliance opinion, passes.

findings.title: The field-completeness test can fail correct entries for the undated note and the notes-to-self, which have no date or no conventional recipient
findings.explanation: C-043 fails the whole log if any entry is missing two or more of these fields: identifier, date, author, recipient, type/description, basis. DOC_017 is an undated handwritten note with no recipient, and the draft log itself records "Recipient: Unknown" with a blank date. DOC_013 is Frey emailing herself. A correct entry for DOC_017 would read "Undated" and "None (note to file)." A strict judge could treat those as two missing fields and fail an otherwise excellent log. The criterion also merges "document type/description" into one field, which makes counting to six unclear.

evidence.quote: **Date of Original:** Undated; no date appears on the original document
E18='Unknown' | F18='Handwritten note (transcribed)'
FAIL if any log entry is missing 2 or more of these 6 fields.

findings.suggested_fix: State that "Undated," "None/Unknown," or "N/A" with an explanation counts as completing the field where the document genuinely lacks that information.

findings.title: C-012 asks for an "approximately 80%" business-content figure that appears nowhere in the record
findings.explanation: C-012 passes if the report notes "that approximately 80% of the email is technical/business discussion with a legal question embedded in one paragraph." The record describes DOC_003 only as "mostly technical" with a legal question "embedded near end." No percentage appears. Most judges will probably accept "predominantly technical, with one paragraph seeking legal advice," and the figure is roughly accurate (about 78% by word count). Still, a literal judge could require a quantitative share the solver had no reason to give.

findings.suggested_fix: Replace the percentage with "predominantly technical/business discussion, with the legal question confined to a single paragraph (or equivalent)."

findings.title: The criteria use a hidden DOC_001-DOC_018 numbering, and the draft log's "priority batch" lists a different 18-file set
findings.explanation: The criteria refer to documents as DOC_003, DOC_009, DOC_014 and so on. That numbering never appears in the instructions or the record, and the draft log's "DOC ID" column is blank. A solver will number the files its own way, for example alphabetically, where DOC_009 would be the clawback memo rather than the Moritani forward. A judge who reads the report's labels against the criteria's labels could mismatch documents. The filenames included in most criteria reduce this risk. Separately, the draft log's Review Notes list 18 "priority batch" files, and about eight of them (e.g., brandt-qa-testing-report.xlsx, tsao-rennick-strategy-email.eml, frey-expert-retention-memo.docx) are not among the 18 supplied documents. Its metadata also conflicts with the supplied files: the Moritani forward is dated 01/12/2025 and the Kovacs email 02/01/2025. This could confuse what "all 18 documents" means, although the instructions clearly refer to the attached files.

blind.overall: Most of the rubric is sound. The criteria follow the supplied privilege-review protocol closely, and their legal propositions are reasonable for N.D. Cal. federal privilege law: third-party waiver, overbroad Slack distribution, privilege stamps not creating privilege, the crime-fraud exception and in camera review, FRE 502(b) factors, common-interest prudence, and not treating the 2021 Pemberton advice as work product. The main defects are factual. C-006 depends on a "near-verbatim" reproduction of the strategy memo in the board deck, but the deck only paraphrases the memo and diverges from it in places. C-014 depends on Fontaine and Chu being cc'd on DOC_003, but the email header shows only Brandt. Either could fail a careful, record-faithful answer under the all-pass metric. Several other criteria are arguable. C-005 assumes DOC_009 forwarded DOC_008 in full, when the two emails differ. C-019's bar on describing the subject matter of the Pemberton letter is stricter than the rules require. C-043's field test can fail correct entries for undated or recipient-less documents, and C-012 asks for an 80% figure that is not in the record. The hidden DOC numbering adds minor grading ambiguity.

sol_verdicts.reason: I agree C-014 is defective, and for a stronger reason than Sol gives. The DOC_003 header lists Tomas Brandt as the only cc. Fontaine and Chu are only named in the body, and only the draft log claims they were cc'd. C-014 therefore requires a factual finding that the primary document contradicts. Sol's own point also holds. The body gives the analysts tasks tied to the reformulation, so the criterion's required conclusion that they "did not need legal advice" is unsupported. Either defect can fail a careful, record-faithful answer.

Nandakumar posted a bare "FYI team" legal conclusion to a 23-member channel that includes warehouse staff, sales reps and a marketing intern. The protocol calls interns and unrelated departments "a red flag," and a sales rep replied that he would tell retail partners. C-021 is already hedged ("likely destroyed"). Treating the post as unprotected or producible is a well-supported need-to-know judgment, not an overstatement. Competent reviewers would not reasonably withhold this message as fully privileged.

None of these criteria claims the Ninth Circuit requires a writing. C-028 says "some jurisdictions require or strongly prefer," which tracks protocol §5(c), and its core demand is flagging the missing writing as a risk. The protocol directs flagging the missing agreement as a risk and designating the email "Privileged — Withhold with Caveats," which is what C-029 requires. The protocol and the draft log both raise formalizing the agreement, so C-047's recommendation to execute a written agreement is ordinary best practice.

Sol's choice-of-law point is fair. The claims are CLRA/UCL/FAL only, so FRE 501 arguably points to California privilege law. The criteria survive under either body of law. California also uses a dominant-purpose test and a crime-fraud exception (Evid. Code 956), and C-013 accepts an "equivalent" framework. C-046 can be passed by stating the standard alone. Costco and §915 limit compelled disclosure; they do not stop the holder from requesting in camera review. The protocol expressly directs that recommendation for borderline documents.

The PASS/FAIL gaps exist: C-043 does not say what happens when an entry is missing one field, and C-045 does not say what happens when one or two documents are omitted. The C-043 gap matters for competent work because DOC_017 (undated, no recipient) and DOC_013 (a note to self) cannot fill every field, so a strict judge could fail a correct log. The C-045 gap mostly affects incomplete answers. It also combines with the hidden DOC_### numbering. I rate both arguable, not confirmed.

C-019 fails any entry saying the advice concerned whether labeling "complied." Yet C-038 and the protocol approve "legal analysis regarding product labeling compliance," and Rule 26(b)(5) requires enough subject matter to assess the claim. That puts compliant subject descriptions at risk. C-020 is fine. It bars only disclosure of specific regulatory conclusions, citric-acid concentrations or FDA thresholds from the billing narratives, which a generic invoice entry easily avoids.

final.changes_from_blind:
Changes after reading Sol:

- **O2 (C-014), revised:** added Sol's point that the \"did not need legal advice\" conclusion is unsupported, on top of my header-conflict finding. It stays problematic.
- **O4 (C-019), revised:** recategorized as an internal inconsistency with C-038 and linked to Sol's B6-PR-6. I dropped the implied concern about C-020, which I judge sound.
- **O5 (C-043), revised:** merged in Sol's point that the PASS and FAIL thresholds leave a gap.
- **O7 (C-045), revised:** added Sol's point that C-045 defines no outcome for one or two omissions. I dropped C-012 from O7's criteria list because O6 covers it.

Sol findings I rejected as not defects:

- **B6-PR-2 (Slack waiver):** the record strongly supports treating the post as unprotected.
- **B6-PR-3 (common interest):** the criteria follow protocol §5 and do not misstate Ninth Circuit law.
- **B6-PR-4 (choice of law and in camera review):** the criteria survive under California law, and the holder may request in camera review voluntarily.

No blind findings were dropped.
final.overall:
The rubric mostly follows the supplied protocol, and its legal positions are defensible. Two criteria depend on facts the record contradicts and could zero out a careful, record-faithful answer under the all-pass metric. C-006 and C-007 depend on a \"near-verbatim\" reproduction of the strategy memo, but the deck paraphrases the memo and diverges from it. C-014 requires Fontaine and Chu to have been cc'd and to have had no need for legal advice, but the header shows only Brandt, and the analysts' need-to-know is unresolved. The arguable issues are:

- C-005/C-003 assume DOC_009 forwarded DOC_008 verbatim, but the two emails differ.
- C-019's wording ban conflicts with C-038.
- C-043's field test is gapped and handles undated or recipient-less documents poorly.
- C-012 asks for an 80% figure not in the record.
- The hidden DOC numbering and C-045's threshold gap add ambiguity.

Sol's waiver, common-interest and choice-of-law challenges do not hold up against the record and the governing law.
